solution:
Boiling point rises with molecular mass (more surface contact, stronger van der Waals forces) and falls with branching, because a branched molecule is more nearly spherical and presents a smaller surface area (Fig. 15.4 of this chapter). n-Pentane is the only \(\mathrm{C_5}\) straight chain in the list, so it should top the list on both counts, and Table 15.2 of this chapter confirms it with measured values:

| Compound | Option | b.p. / K |
|---|---|---|
| Pentane (n-pentane) | a | 309.1 |
| 2,2-Dimethylpropane (neopentane) | d | 282.5 |
| Butane | c | 272.4 |
| 2-Methylpropane (iso-butane) | b | 261.0 |

Every alternative fails on the table's own numbers. Neopentane is \(\mathrm{C_5H_{12}}\) like n-pentane but is doubly branched, and boils 26.6 K lower. Butane and iso-butane are \(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}\), one carbon shorter, and boil lower still; iso-butane is the branched one of that pair and is the lowest boiling of all four. So n-pentane has the highest boiling point.

Acetylene, \(\mathrm{H-C \equiv C-H}\), is a terminal alkyne: its hydrogen is bonded directly to an sp hybridised carbon. As this chapter explains, an sp hybrid orbital has 50% s-character, so its electrons are held close to the nucleus and the sp carbon is more electronegative than the \(\mathrm{sp^2}\) carbon of ethene or the \(\mathrm{sp^3}\) carbon of ethane. That polarises the C–H bond enough for the hydrogen to be given up as \(\mathrm{H^+}\) to a very strong base — acetylene reacts with lithium amide to give lithium acetylide with loss of \(\mathrm{NH_3}\).

The other three have no such hydrogen. In ethane, \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_3}\), the carbons are \(\mathrm{sp^3}\) (25% s-character) and in ethylene, \(\mathrm{CH_2=CH_2}\), they are \(\mathrm{sp^2}\) (33%); this chapter's own note says alkanes and alkenes do not react with lithium amide. Dimethyl acetylene is but-2-yne, \(\mathrm{CH_3-C \equiv C-CH_3}\) — it does contain a triple bond, but both triple-bonded carbons carry a methyl group, so there is no hydrogen on an sp carbon at all. Acidic hydrogen is therefore present only in acetylene.

The printed products are propanone (acetone), \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2O}\), so the double bond has been cleaved right through and one fragment has been oxidised all the way to carbon dioxide. This chapter's oxidation section says alkenes treated with acidic \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) form ketones and/or acids, and gives exactly this pattern in its own worked examples: prop-1-ene gives ethanoic acid \(+\ \mathrm{CO_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\), and 2-methylbut-2-ene gives propan-2-one and ethanoic acid. Applying it to 2-methylprop-1-ene, \(\mathrm{CH_3-C(CH_3)=CH_2}\), the disubstituted carbon becomes the ketone \(\mathrm{CH_3-CO-CH_3}\) and the terminal \(\mathrm{=CH_2}\), which carries two hydrogens, is oxidised past the acid stage to \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2O}\). Reagent 'A' is acidified potassium permanganate.

None of the other reagents cleaves the double bond. Cold dilute alkaline \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) is Baeyer's reagent and only hydroxylates the alkene, giving 2-methylpropane-1,2-diol with the carbon skeleton intact and no \(\mathrm{CO_2}\). Dilute \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) with 1% \(\mathrm{HgSO_4}\) is the reagent this chapter uses for hydration of alkynes; on an alkene it could at most add water across the double bond to give an alcohol. \(\mathrm{NaOH/H_2O_2}\) is the oxidative work-up used after hydroboration and also yields an alcohol, not a ketone plus carbon dioxide.

Ethylbenzene is \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-C_2H_5}\). This chapter lists \(\mathrm{CH_3}\), \(\mathrm{C_2H_5}\) and R among the ortho and para directing groups, so chlorination must put the incoming chlorine at an ortho or a para position, and the meta product is not the major one. Chlorobenzene cannot form at all: it would require the ethyl group to be stripped off the ring, and electrophilic substitution replaces a ring hydrogen, never an alkyl substituent.

That leaves the ortho and the para isomers, both of which are genuinely formed. The para product is the major one because the two ortho positions lie immediately beside the bulky ethyl group and attack there is sterically hindered, whereas the para position is free. So the major product is p-chloroethylbenzene.

[Note: this chapter groups ortho and para products together and does not itself rank one above the other, so the choice between the two rests on the steric argument above rather than on a statement in the text. The ortho isomer is a real minor product, not an impossible one.]

Hot concentrated alcoholic KOH brings about dehydrohalogenation — this chapter's \(\beta\)-elimination, in which the halogen leaves the \(\alpha\)-carbon and a hydrogen leaves the adjacent \(\beta\)-carbon, so an alkene is formed. The chapter's own examples are bromoethane giving ethene and 2-chlorobutane giving butene. With 1-chloropropane, \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2Cl}\), the only \(\beta\)-carbon bearing hydrogen is C-2, so \(\mathrm{HCl}\) is eliminated across C-1 and C-2:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2Cl + KOH \ (alcoholic)}\) \(\xrightarrow{\text{boil}}\) \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH_2 + KCl + H_2O}\)

Propane would need the chlorine to be replaced by hydrogen, which is a reduction (Zn and dilute HCl in this chapter), not the action of a base. Propyne would need two molecules of hydrogen halide removed, and this chapter obtains alkynes from vicinal DIhalides, not from a monohalide. Propyl alcohol is the substitution product formed when the halide is hydrolysed by aqueous alkali; the alcoholic medium specified here is what steers the reaction to elimination instead. The product is propene.
